CHN-02.Route planning: Deciding the paths and schedules delivery vehicles will follow so goods arrive on time at the lowest cost.
CHN-02.Customer service: In logistics, meeting customers' delivery needs by getting orders to them complete, undamaged and on time, and fixing problems.
CHN-02.Cross-docking: Moving goods straight from an arriving truck to a departing one at a distribution center, with little or no storage in between.
CHN-02.Reverse logistics: Moving goods backward through the channel, from customers to the seller, for returns, repairs, recycling or disposal.
CHN-02.Containerization: Packing goods into large standard containers that can be moved between ships, trains and trucks without being unpacked.

CHN-03.Broker: An intermediary that brings a buyer and seller together to make a deal and earns a fee, without owning or usually handling the goods.
CHN-03.Merchant wholesaler: An independent wholesaler that buys goods and takes title to them, meaning it owns them, before reselling to other businesses.
CHN-03.Manufacturers agent: An independent agent who sells related, non-competing products for several manufacturers in a set territory, paid by commission.
CHN-03.Full-service wholesaler: A merchant wholesaler that offers a full range of services, such as storage, delivery, credit and sales help.
CHN-03.Limited-service wholesaler: A merchant wholesaler that offers only a few services to its customers and usually charges lower prices as a result.
CHN-03.Drop shipper: A limited-service wholesaler that owns the goods it sells but never handles them, since the producer ships directly to the buyer.
CHN-03.Cash-and-carry wholesaler: A limited-service wholesaler whose customers come to it, pay on the spot and take the goods away themselves. No credit or delivery.
CHN-03.Industrial distributor: A merchant wholesaler that sells equipment, parts and supplies to manufacturers and other businesses, not to retailers.
CHN-03.Rack jobber: A wholesaler that supplies, stocks and manages its own display racks in retail stores, usually for non-food items.
CHN-03.Truck jobber: A limited-service wholesaler that sells and delivers goods, often perishable ones, straight from a truck on a regular route.
CHN-03.Selling agent: An agent that handles the marketing of a producer's entire output, often with a say over prices and terms.
CHN-03.General merchandise wholesaler: A full-service wholesaler that carries a broad mix of unrelated product lines, such as hardware, clothing and cosmetics.
CHN-03.Specialty wholesaler: A wholesaler that carries only part of one product line but offers great depth and expert knowledge within it.
CHN-03.Export agent: An agent that finds foreign buyers for a home producer's goods and arranges the sale for a commission. An import agent does the reverse.
CHN-03.Purchasing agent: An agent that buys goods on behalf of a client business, often over a long relationship, and is paid a fee or commission.
CHN-03.Commission merchant: An agent that takes physical possession of goods, usually farm products, sells them at the best price and keeps a commission.
CHN-03.Mail-order wholesaler: A limited-service wholesaler that sells to small business customers from a catalog and ships orders by mail or carrier.
CHN-03.Auction company: An agent that provides a place where goods are displayed and sold to the highest bidder, earning a fee or commission.
CHN-03.Manufacturers sales branch: A wholesaling operation owned and run by the manufacturer itself, selling its goods without independent wholesalers.
CHN-03.Single-line wholesaler: A full-service wholesaler that carries a complete assortment within one line of goods, such as groceries or hardware.
CHN-03.Producers cooperative: A wholesaling business owned by its farmer members, which gathers and sells their produce and shares the profits among them.

CHN-04.Transporting: Physically moving the goods from the producer toward the places where customers can buy them.
CHN-04.Selling: Presenting the product to buyers and persuading them to purchase, so the producer does not need a sales force in every area.
CHN-04.Storing: Holding goods in warehouses or stockrooms until customers want them, so products are available when needed.
CHN-04.Promotion: Advertising and displaying the producer's goods to local customers and telling them about the products.
CHN-04.Buying: Purchasing goods from producers, usually in large quantities, which gives the producer a sure sale and money sooner.
CHN-04.Customer service: Helping buyers after the sale with things like installation, repairs, returns and answers to questions.
CHN-04.Financing: Providing the money or credit that keeps goods moving, such as paying the producer before the goods are resold or giving customers credit.
CHN-04.Market information: Passing on what they learn about customers, competitors and sales trends, which helps the producer plan products and prices.
CHN-04.Order processing: Taking customers' orders and handling the paperwork and steps needed to fill and deliver them.
CHN-04.Displaying products: Placing goods on shelves and in displays where shoppers can see, compare and pick them up.
CHN-04.Breaking bulk: Buying in large lots from producers and dividing them into the smaller quantities that retailers or consumers want.
CHN-04.Risk bearing: Accepting the chance of loss that comes with owning goods, such as theft, damage, spoilage or items that do not sell.
CHN-04.Negotiation: Working out prices, quantities, delivery and other terms so that ownership of the goods can pass from seller to buyer.
CHN-04.Finding customers: Locating likely buyers and making contact with them, so the producer's goods are matched with people who want them.
CHN-04.Repackaging: Putting goods received in bulk into smaller or more suitable packages and labeling them for the next buyer.
CHN-04.Assorting: Bringing together a mix of different products from many producers, so customers can get everything they need in one place.
CHN-04.Grading: Sorting products into classes by quality or size and labeling them to a standard, so buyers know what they are getting.
CHN-04.Accumulating: Collecting small amounts of similar goods from many producers into one larger supply that is cheaper to ship and sell.

CHN-05.Direct distribution: The producer sells straight to the final customer with no intermediaries, for example through its own website or stores.
CHN-05.Indirect distribution: The producer reaches customers through one or more intermediaries, such as wholesalers and retailers.
CHN-05.Online channel: Selling through a website, app or online marketplace, with goods delivered to the buyer instead of bought in a shop.
CHN-05.Exclusive distribution: Giving a single dealer the sole right to sell the product in an area. Used for luxury goods such as high-end cars.
CHN-05.Intensive distribution: Placing the product in as many outlets as possible so it is always within reach. Used for convenience goods such as snacks.
CHN-05.Selective distribution: Using a limited number of chosen outlets in each area. Suited to shopping goods such as appliances and branded clothing.
CHN-05.Franchising: A producer or brand owner licenses independent owners to sell its goods or run its business format under its name, for fees.
CHN-05.Multichannel distribution: Using two or more different channels at once to reach customers, such as the producer's own website, retail stores and a catalog.
CHN-05.Agent channel: Using agents or brokers, who do not own the goods, to find buyers and arrange sales for the producer on commission.
CHN-05.Drop shipping: An arrangement where the seller takes the order but the producer or a wholesaler ships the goods directly to the customer.
CHN-05.Omnichannel: Linking every channel, such as stores, website, app and social media, so customers get one smooth experience across all of them.
CHN-05.Vertical integration: One company owning more than one level of the channel, such as a manufacturer that buys its suppliers or opens its own stores.
CHN-05.Conventional channel: A channel of independent producers, wholesalers and retailers, each a separate business seeking its own profit with little coordination.
CHN-05.Vertical marketing system: A channel in which producer, wholesaler and retailer work as one unified system, led by one member through ownership, contract or power.
CHN-05.Horizontal marketing system: Two or more companies at the same channel level joining forces to pursue an opportunity, such as a bank branch inside a supermarket.
CHN-05.Contractual VMS: A vertical marketing system (VMS) in which independent firms at different levels are tied together by contracts, as in franchising.
CHN-05.Administered VMS: A vertical marketing system (VMS) coordinated by the size and power of one dominant member, not by ownership or contract.

CHN-06.Shopping mall: A large, usually enclosed center with many stores under one roof, anchored by department stores and surrounded by parking.
CHN-06.Strip mall: A row of stores side by side facing a shared parking lot, usually serving the nearby neighborhood with everyday goods and services.
CHN-06.Downtown: The central business district of a town or city, where shops benefit from office workers, public transportation and foot traffic.
CHN-06.Outlet mall: A shopping center made up mostly of manufacturers' and retailers' outlet stores selling brand-name goods at reduced prices.
CHN-06.Freestanding location: A store in its own building that is not attached to other shops. It has good visibility and parking but must draw its own customers.
CHN-06.Transit hub: A site inside an airport, train station or bus terminal, where shops sell to the steady flow of travelers passing through.
CHN-06.Kiosk: A small stand or booth in a busy walkway, such as a mall corridor, that needs little space and low rent.
CHN-06.Lifestyle center: An open-air shopping center with upscale specialty shops, restaurants and entertainment, designed to feel like a pleasant main street.
CHN-06.Power center: A large open-air center made up mainly of several big-box stores and category killers, with few small shops.
CHN-06.Community shopping center: A mid-sized center, larger than a strip mall and smaller than a regional mall, often anchored by a supermarket or discount store.
CHN-06.Pop-up location: A space used for only a short time, such as an empty storefront or event stall, for a seasonal or trial store.
CHN-06.Nontraditional location: A site not normally thought of as retail space, such as a hospital, college campus, stadium or office building.
CHN-06.Flea market: An open market where many independent sellers rent stalls or tables to sell new and used goods, often on weekends.
CHN-06.Store within a store: A branded shop set up inside a larger retailer's store, in space the brand rents or shares, such as a cosmetics counter.
CHN-06.Mixed-use development: A project that combines shops with offices, housing or hotels in one place, giving stores a built-in supply of customers.
CHN-06.Super-regional center: The largest kind of mall, with three or more anchor department stores and a huge number of shops, drawing people from far away.
CHN-06.Secondary business district: A smaller shopping area away from downtown, usually at a major street intersection, serving one part of a city.
CHN-06.Festival marketplace: A shopping and entertainment center built around a theme or historic site, with restaurants and specialty shops aimed at tourists.

MKR-01.Survey: Asking a group of people the same set of questions, by web, phone, mail or in person. The most common way to collect primary data.
MKR-01.Focus group: A guided discussion with a small group, usually 6 to 12 people, led by a moderator to explore their opinions in depth.
MKR-01.Interview: A one-on-one conversation in which a researcher asks a person questions and can probe for detailed answers.
MKR-01.Observation: Watching and recording what people actually do, such as how shoppers move through a store, without asking them questions.
MKR-01.Experiment: Changing one factor, such as price or packaging, while keeping the rest the same, to see how it affects what people do.
MKR-01.Comment cards: Short forms customers fill in to rate their experience and leave suggestions, often found on tables or at the checkout.
MKR-01.Taste test: Having people try a product, often without knowing the brand, and give their reactions or say which one they prefer.
MKR-01.Mystery shopper: A person hired to pose as an ordinary customer and report back on service, cleanliness and how the visit went.
MKR-01.Consumer panel: A group of people who agree to give information repeatedly over time, showing how their opinions and buying habits change.
MKR-01.Test marketing: Selling a new product in a few chosen areas first, to see how real customers respond before launching it everywhere.
MKR-01.Website analytics: Data a business collects on how visitors use its own website, such as pages viewed, clicks and time spent.
MKR-01.Ethnographic research: Studying people closely in their own homes or workplaces to see how products fit into their everyday lives.
MKR-01.Diary study: Asking people to keep a written record over days or weeks of what they buy, use, watch or do.

MKR-02.Internet: Websites, articles and search results that already contain facts and figures on markets, industries and customers. Sources must be checked.
MKR-02.Census data: Official counts of a country's population, with details such as age, income and household size for each area.
MKR-02.Government agencies: Public bodies that publish free statistics and reports on the economy, industries, trade and population.
MKR-02.Company records: Information the business already holds, such as sales figures, customer lists and financial statements. Called internal secondary data.
MKR-02.Libraries: Collections of books, reference works, directories and databases that researchers can consult, often for free.
MKR-02.Newspapers: News articles and business magazines that report on companies, trends, the economy and local markets.
MKR-02.Trade associations: Organizations of businesses in the same industry, which collect and share statistics and reports about that industry.
MKR-02.Trade publications: Magazines and journals written for people in one industry, covering its trends, sales figures, competitors and new products.
MKR-02.Industry reports: Published studies that describe the size, growth, trends and main competitors of a particular industry or market.
MKR-02.Online databases: Searchable electronic collections of articles, statistics and company information, often available by subscription.
MKR-02.Previous research studies: Studies that were carried out earlier, by the business or by others, whose results can be used again.
MKR-02.Commercial research firms: Companies that collect data on markets and consumers and sell it to many clients. Data sold this way is called syndicated data.
MKR-02.Academic journals: Publications of research by university scholars, reviewed by other experts before being printed.
MKR-02.Competitor annual reports: Yearly documents in which publicly traded rival companies describe their finances, strategies and plans, open for anyone to read.
MKR-02.Chamber of commerce: A local association of businesses that keeps information on the area's economy, population and member companies.
MKR-02.Bureau of Labor Statistics: The United States government agency that publishes data on employment, wages, prices and consumer spending.
MKR-02.SEC filings: Reports that public companies must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), such as the yearly 10-K, revealing their finances.

MKR-03.Define the problem: The first step: stating clearly what the business needs to find out or decide, so the research stays focused.
MKR-03.Collect data: Carrying out the research by gathering the information, through surveys, interviews, observation or existing sources.
MKR-03.Analyze data: Studying the collected information to find patterns and meaning, turning raw numbers and answers into useful findings.
MKR-03.Recommend solutions: Drawing conclusions from the analysis and suggesting what the business should do about the problem.
MKR-03.Present findings: Reporting the results to the decision makers, usually in a written report or presentation with charts and a summary.
MKR-03.Develop research plan: Deciding how the research will be done, including what data is needed, which methods to use, who to ask and the cost.
MKR-03.Set research objectives: Stating exactly what the research is meant to achieve, which turns the problem into specific questions to answer.
MKR-03.Implement findings: Putting the recommendations into action and checking later whether the change solved the problem.
MKR-03.Select sample: Choosing which people, and how many, will be studied so that they fairly represent the whole group of interest.
MKR-03.Review secondary data: Checking information that already exists before collecting new data, since it may answer the question more cheaply.
MKR-03.Identify information needed: Working out exactly which facts are required to solve the problem and where they can be found.
MKR-03.Develop hypothesis: Writing a testable statement of what the researcher expects to find, which the data will then support or reject.
MKR-03.Design questionnaire: Writing and arranging the survey questions so they are clear, unbiased and gather exactly the data required.
MKR-03.Process the data: Checking, editing, coding and tabulating the raw answers so they are accurate and ready to be analyzed.
MKR-03.Pretest the survey: Trying the questionnaire on a small group first, to catch confusing or faulty questions before the full study.

MKR-04.Random sampling: Every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen, like drawing names from a hat. It limits bias.
MKR-04.Convenience sampling: Choosing whoever is easiest to reach, such as shoppers walking by. Quick and cheap, but the sample may not represent the population.
MKR-04.Stratified sampling: Dividing the population into groups, such as age bands, and drawing a random sample from every group so each is represented.
MKR-04.Cluster sampling: Dividing the population into groups, such as city blocks, randomly choosing some of the groups, and studying people only in those.
MKR-04.Systematic sampling: Picking a random starting point on a list and then choosing every nth name, such as every tenth customer.
MKR-04.Probability sampling: The family of methods in which every member of the population has a known chance of selection, so results can be generalized.
MKR-04.Quota sampling: Choosing people non-randomly until set numbers from certain groups are filled, such as 50 men and 50 women.
MKR-04.Judgment sampling: The researcher hand-picks the people believed to be best suited to the study, relying on personal expertise instead of chance.
MKR-04.Voluntary response sampling: People decide for themselves whether to take part, as in an online poll. Those with strong opinions are over-represented.
MKR-04.Nonprobability sampling: The family of methods in which people are not chosen by chance, so some have no known chance of selection and bias is more likely.
MKR-04.Snowball sampling: Asking each participant to suggest other people who qualify, so the sample grows through referrals. Useful for hard-to-find groups.
MKR-04.Multistage sampling: Sampling in two or more steps, such as randomly choosing cities, then neighborhoods within them, then households.
MKR-04.Random digit dialing: Having a computer generate telephone numbers at random for a phone survey, so unlisted numbers can be reached too.

MKR-05.Multiple choice: A question that gives a list of possible answers and asks the respondent to choose one. Easy to answer and to count.
MKR-05.Yes or no: A question with only two possible answers, also called a dichotomous question. Simple, but it gives no detail.
MKR-05.Open-ended: A question people answer in their own words, with no choices given. It yields rich detail but is harder to tabulate.
MKR-05.Rating scale: A question asking people to score something along a range, such as from 1 to 5 or from poor to excellent.
MKR-05.Closed-ended: Any question that limits respondents to a fixed set of answers, which makes the results quick to count and compare.
MKR-05.Ranking: A question asking respondents to put several items in order, such as from most important to least important.
MKR-05.Likert scale: A scale that asks how strongly a person agrees or disagrees with a statement, usually over five points.
MKR-05.Demographic question: A question about facts describing the respondent, such as age, gender or income, used to sort answers into groups.
MKR-05.Fill in the blank: A question with a gap in a sentence that the respondent completes with a word or short phrase of their own.
MKR-05.Checklist: A question that lists several options and lets the respondent check every one that applies, not just one.
MKR-05.Net promoter score: A question asking how likely a customer is, from 0 to 10, to recommend the business to others. A measure of loyalty.
MKR-05.Semantic differential: A scale with opposite words at each end, such as modern and old-fashioned, where respondents mark a point between them.
MKR-05.Filter question: A question that screens respondents, sending those who qualify on to later questions and letting the rest skip them.
MKR-05.Matrix question: A grid that lists several items in rows and uses the same answer scale in the columns for all of them.
MKR-05.Constant sum: A question asking respondents to divide a fixed total, such as 100 points, among several items to show how important each is.

MKR-06.Small sample size: Too few people were surveyed, so the results may reflect chance and not the views of the whole population.
MKR-06.Leading question: A question worded in a way that pushes the respondent toward a particular answer, such as asking how much they loved the service.
MKR-06.Unrepresentative sample: The people surveyed differ from the population being studied, so their answers cannot fairly stand in for everyone.
MKR-06.Dishonest answers: Respondents give untrue answers, perhaps out of embarrassment, to please the researcher or simply to finish quickly.
MKR-06.Low response rate: Only a small share of the people asked actually answer. Those who reply may differ from those who do not.
MKR-06.Confusing wording: Questions that are vague, use jargon or can be read in more than one way, so people answer different questions without knowing it.
MKR-06.Interviewer bias: The interviewer's tone, appearance, wording or reactions influence how respondents answer.
MKR-06.Sampling error: The natural gap between a sample's results and the true figure for the whole population, which exists because not everyone was asked.
MKR-06.Voluntary response bias: When people choose for themselves whether to take part, those with strong feelings respond most and skew the results.
MKR-06.Double-barreled question: A question that asks about two things at once, such as price and quality, so it is unclear which one the answer refers to.
MKR-06.Loaded question: A question containing emotional words or a built-in assumption that makes one answer seem right or the other unacceptable.
MKR-06.Social desirability bias: Respondents give the answer that makes them look good, not the true one, for example overstating how often they exercise.
MKR-06.Recall error: Respondents cannot remember past events accurately, such as what they bought last month, and so give wrong answers.
MKR-06.Undercoverage: Some groups in the population are left out of the list the sample is drawn from, so their views are missing from the results.
MKR-06.Limited answer choices: The options provided do not include a respondent's real answer, forcing them to pick one that does not fit.
MKR-06.Question order: Earlier questions affect how people answer later ones, for example by putting a certain idea in their minds.
MKR-06.Data entry error: Mistakes made when answers are recorded, typed in, coded or counted, which make the data wrong after it was collected.
MKR-06.Respondent fatigue: People get tired or bored during a long survey and start answering carelessly, skipping questions or quitting.
MKR-06.Acquiescence bias: The tendency of some respondents to agree with statements or say yes, whatever the question actually asks.

MKR-07.Name: The customer's first and last name, the basic identifier of the record, used to address them personally.
MKR-07.Email address: Where the business sends receipts, order updates and marketing messages. Often the main way of keeping in touch.
MKR-07.Phone number: A number for calling or texting the customer about orders, appointments, service problems or offers.
MKR-07.Purchase history: A record of what the customer has bought, when and for how much. It reveals their habits and suggests what to offer next.
MKR-07.Mailing address: The customer's street address, used for deliveries, bills and mailed offers and for seeing where customers are located.
MKR-07.Birthday: The customer's date of birth, used to send birthday greetings or offers and to work out their age group.
MKR-07.Preferences: The customer's likes, such as favorite products, sizes, styles or interests, which let the business tailor its recommendations.
MKR-07.Payment information: How the customer pays, such as a saved card or billing details, which speeds up checkout. It must be kept secure.
MKR-07.Demographics: Facts describing the customer, such as age, gender, income and occupation, used to group customers into segments.
MKR-07.Loyalty points: The customer's rewards balance and membership level in the loyalty program, showing how much they have earned and can redeem.
MKR-07.Service history: A record of past complaints, returns, repairs and support requests, so staff know what problems the customer has had.
MKR-07.Account number: A unique code given to each customer so that their record can be found quickly and never confused with another.
MKR-07.Company name: The organization the customer works for or buys on behalf of. An essential field when selling to other businesses.
MKR-07.Contact history: A log of every call, email, meeting and chat with the customer, so any employee can see what was said before.
MKR-07.Communication preferences: How and whether the customer wants to be contacted, such as by email or text, and whether they agreed to marketing.
MKR-07.Website activity: What the customer does online with the business, such as pages viewed, items left in a cart and emails opened.
MKR-07.Social media profiles: The customer's social media accounts and how they interact with the brand there, such as comments and mentions.
MKR-07.Lead source: How the customer first found the business, such as an ad, a referral or a trade show. It shows which marketing works.
MKR-07.Customer lifetime value: An estimate of the total money the customer will bring the business over the whole relationship, showing who is worth most.
MKR-07.Satisfaction scores: The customer's ratings and survey answers about their experience, which flag unhappy customers before they leave.
MKR-07.Lead status: Where a potential customer stands in the sales process, such as new, contacted, qualified or close to buying.

BRD-01.Logo: The symbol or design that identifies a brand at a glance. The part that can be seen but not spoken is also called the brand mark.
BRD-01.Brand name: The word, letters or numbers of a brand that can be spoken, used to identify a product or company.
BRD-01.Slogan: A short, catchy phrase linked with a brand that sums up its message or promise and is easy to remember.
BRD-01.Colors: The particular colors a brand uses again and again, so people come to recognize it by color alone.
BRD-01.Jingle: A short tune or song used in a brand's advertising that sticks in people's minds and makes them think of the brand.
BRD-01.Packaging: The container and its design. A distinctive shape, color or label helps shoppers spot the brand on the shelf.
BRD-01.Trademark: A brand name, symbol or other mark that is legally protected, so only its owner may use it.
BRD-01.Trade character: A person, animal or cartoon figure created to represent a brand, such as a cereal mascot.
BRD-01.Typography: The style of lettering a brand uses in its name and materials. A consistent typeface becomes part of its recognizable look.
BRD-01.Design: The distinctive shape and visual style of a product, which can make it recognizable even without its name.
BRD-01.Trade name: The legal name under which a company does business. It identifies the company itself, not one particular product.
BRD-01.Brand personality: The human traits a brand is given, such as friendly, rugged or sophisticated, shown through its tone and style.
BRD-01.Brand story: The account of where a brand came from and what it stands for, told to help customers feel a connection with it.
BRD-01.Brand values: The principles a brand says it stands for, such as honesty or caring for the environment, which guide how it acts.
BRD-01.Spokesperson: A real person, often a celebrity, who regularly appears for a brand and becomes linked with it in the public's mind.
BRD-01.Brand promise: What a brand tells customers they can expect every time they buy, such as fast delivery or reliable quality.
BRD-01.Trade dress: The overall look of a product or its packaging, such as shape, color and layout, which the law can protect when it identifies the brand.
BRD-01.Domain name: The brand's web address. A name that matches the brand helps people find it online and stops others from using it.

BRD-02.National brand: A brand owned and promoted by the manufacturer that makes the product and sold in many different stores. Also called a manufacturer brand.
BRD-02.Generic brand: A plain product with no brand name or advertising, labeled only by what it is and sold at a low price.
BRD-02.Private label: A brand owned by a retailer or wholesaler and sold only in its own stores, usually priced below national brands. Also called a store brand.
BRD-02.Co-branding: Putting two established brands together on one product, such as a candy brand in an ice cream, so each gains from the other.
BRD-02.Brand extension: Using an existing, successful brand name to launch a product in a new and different category, such as a motorcycle brand selling clothing.
BRD-02.Rebranding: Changing a brand's name, logo, look or message to give it a new image in customers' minds.
BRD-02.Brand licensing: Allowing another company to use a brand name, logo or character on its products in exchange for a fee or royalty.
BRD-02.Family branding: Selling many of a company's products under one shared brand name, so each benefits from the others' reputation.
BRD-02.Line extension: Adding new versions of a product in the same category under the same brand name, such as new flavors, sizes or colors.
BRD-02.Individual branding: Giving each product its own separate brand name, so one product's failure does not harm the others.
BRD-02.New brand: Creating a brand-new name for a product entering a new category, used when none of the company's existing names fits.
BRD-02.Personal brand: The reputation and public image a person builds for themselves, as athletes, entertainers and business leaders do.
BRD-02.Global brand: A brand sold under the same name and with a similar image in many countries around the world.
BRD-02.Multibranding: A company selling two or more different brands in the same product category, each aimed at a different group of buyers.
BRD-02.Mixed branding: A company selling its products both under its own brand name and as private label goods for retailers.
BRD-02.Fighter brand: A lower-priced brand a company launches to compete with cheap rivals while protecting the price and image of its main brand.
BRD-02.Flanker brand: A new brand a company adds in a category where it already sells, to reach a different segment and guard its main brand.
BRD-02.Ingredient branding: Promoting a branded part or material contained inside another company's product, such as a named processor in a laptop.
BRD-02.Endorsed branding: Giving a product its own name while also showing the parent company's name on it as a mark of approval.

BRD-03.Protect the product: Shielding the contents from damage, dirt, moisture and breakage during shipping, storage, display and use.
BRD-03.Promote the product: Catching the shopper's eye with color, shape and design so the product stands out on the shelf and sells itself.
BRD-03.Provide information: Telling the buyer what they need to know, such as ingredients, directions, size, warnings and nutrition facts.
BRD-03.Contain the product: Holding the contents together in one unit, which matters most for liquids, powders and items with many pieces.
BRD-03.Convenience: Making the product easier to carry, open, pour, reseal or use, such as a squeeze bottle or single-serve pack.
BRD-03.Identify the product: Showing clearly which brand and product it is, so shoppers can recognize it and tell it apart from competitors.
BRD-03.Safety: Keeping users from harm with features such as child-resistant caps, tamper-evident seals and shatterproof containers.
BRD-03.Preserve freshness: Keeping air, light and moisture out so food and other perishable products stay fresh and usable for longer.
BRD-03.Storage and shipping: Giving the product a shape and strength that make it easy to stack, store and transport efficiently.
BRD-03.Communicate benefits: Using words and pictures on the package to show what the product does and why it is worth buying.
BRD-03.Theft prevention: Making small, costly items harder to steal, for example with oversized packages or hard plastic shells that hold security tags.
BRD-03.Meet legal requirements: Carrying the information and features the law demands, such as ingredient lists, health warnings and child-resistant closures.
BRD-03.Allow reuse: Being designed so the buyer can use the container again for another purpose, such as a jar that becomes a drinking glass.

BRD-04.Price: Presenting the product as the lowest-cost choice or the best value for money, so shoppers think of it when they want to save.
BRD-04.Quality: Presenting the product as better made, more reliable or longer lasting than the alternatives.
BRD-04.Features: Stressing specific characteristics of the product itself, such as its ingredients, size, speed or design.
BRD-04.Benefits: Stressing what the product does for the customer, such as saving time or preventing cavities, not just what it contains.
BRD-04.Customer service: Standing out for how well the company treats and helps its customers, such as expert advice or generous support.
BRD-04.Convenience: Presenting the product as the easiest or fastest option to get and use, such as quick delivery or many locations.
BRD-04.Competitors: Defining the product by direct comparison with a rival, claiming to be better than or different from that brand.
BRD-04.Use or application: Linking the product with a particular use or occasion, such as a drink for after exercise or a snack for movie nights.
BRD-04.Product user: Linking the product with a particular type of person, such as serious athletes or busy parents.
BRD-04.Lifestyle: Tying the product to a way of living or a feeling that customers want, such as adventure, health or family time.
BRD-04.Uniqueness: Building the position on something no competitor offers, the product's point of difference.
BRD-04.Prestige: Presenting the product as a symbol of status and luxury that is exclusive and worth a high price.
BRD-04.Innovation: Presenting the brand as the leader in new ideas and the latest technology.
BRD-04.Sustainability: Presenting the product as kind to the environment, for example through recycled materials or low-waste production.
BRD-04.Product class: Setting the product against a whole category instead of one rival, such as a spread positioned as an alternative to butter.
BRD-04.Heritage: Building the position on the brand's long history, tradition or place of origin, which suggests trust and authenticity.
BRD-04.Cultural symbol: Positioning through a symbol, character or image that people widely recognize and that comes to stand for the brand.

BRD-05.Brand name: The name, and often the logo, that tells the shopper which company's product it is. Usually the most prominent item on the label.
BRD-05.Ingredients: A list of what the product contains or is made of. On food labels items are listed in order from most to least by weight.
BRD-05.Nutrition facts: A panel on packaged food showing calories and amounts of nutrients such as fat, sugar, protein and sodium per serving.
BRD-05.Price: What the item costs, printed on the label or a tag. A unit price shows the cost per ounce or per item for easy comparison.
BRD-05.Directions for use: Instructions explaining how to use, prepare or take the product correctly and safely.
BRD-05.Expiration date: The date after which the product should not be sold or used, or by which it is at its best quality.
BRD-05.Warnings: Statements alerting users to dangers of the product, such as being flammable, poisonous or unsafe for small children.
BRD-05.Net weight: The amount of product inside, not counting the package, given by weight, volume or count.
BRD-05.Barcode: A pattern of lines that a scanner reads to identify the item at checkout and in stock records. Often a Universal Product Code (UPC).
BRD-05.Product description: Words that say what the item is and which version, such as its flavor, variety, scent or main features.
BRD-05.Country of origin: A statement of where the product was made or grown, such as Made in Canada. Required on many imported goods.
BRD-05.Manufacturer name and address: The name and location of the company that made, packed or distributed the product, so buyers know who is responsible.
BRD-05.Care instructions: Directions for looking after the item, such as how to wash, dry and iron a piece of clothing.
BRD-05.Allergen statement: A notice that the product contains, or may contain, common allergy-causing foods such as nuts, milk, eggs or wheat.
BRD-05.Serving size: The amount of food counted as one serving, on which the nutrition figures are based, with the number of servings in the package.
BRD-05.Certifications: Seals showing that an outside organization has checked the product against a standard, such as organic, kosher or fair trade.
BRD-05.Recycling symbol: A mark showing that the package can be recycled, often with a code for the type of material it is made from.
BRD-05.Storage instructions: Directions on how to keep the product so it stays safe and fresh, such as refrigerate after opening.
BRD-05.Contact information: A phone number, website or address that customers can use to reach the company with questions or complaints.
BRD-05.Grade: A rating of the product's quality set against an official standard, such as Grade A on eggs.
BRD-05.Lot number: A code identifying the batch in which the item was made, used to trace and recall products if a problem is found.
BRD-05.Age recommendation: The ages the product is suitable for, common on toys and games, such as ages 3 and up.
BRD-05.Model number: A code that identifies the exact version of a product, needed when ordering parts, registering a warranty or seeking service.

BRD-06.Brand awareness: How well customers know that a brand exists and can recognize or remember it. The base on which brand equity is built.
BRD-06.Brand loyalty: Customers' commitment to keep buying one brand over others. Loyal buyers bring steady sales and resist rivals' offers.
BRD-06.Brand recognition: The level at which customers know the brand when they see or hear it and can tell it apart from others.
BRD-06.Brand preference: The level at which customers choose the brand over competitors when it is available, but will accept a substitute if it is not.
BRD-06.Perceived quality: Customers' own opinion of how good a brand's products are, whether or not it matches the actual quality.
BRD-06.Brand associations: The thoughts, feelings and images that come to mind when people think of a brand, such as safety or fun.
BRD-06.Brand insistence: The level at which customers demand one brand, accept no substitute and will go out of their way to find it.
BRD-06.Brand recall: Customers' ability to name the brand from memory when given only the product category, without seeing it.
BRD-06.Brand rejection: The level at which customers know the brand but refuse to buy it, usually because of its poor image.
BRD-06.Brand nonrecognition: The level at which customers do not recognize the brand at all, so the name does nothing to help sell the product.
BRD-06.Proprietary brand assets: Things a brand legally owns that protect it from competitors, such as patents, trademarks and channel relationships.
BRD-06.Brand resonance: The deepest bond between customers and a brand, shown by strong loyalty, attachment and a sense of community around it.
